title: Lando Norris Calls for FIA Race Ban After Franco Colapinto’s Baku Crash – Motorsport.com Report
body:
Lando Norris, the 2023 World Champion, called for a one‑race suspension for rookie driver Franco Colapinto after the Argentine’s mistake on the restart of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix caused a multi‑car pile‑up that eliminated both Norris’s McLaren and Alpine’s Pierre Gasly. The incident, which unfolded on lap 36 of the Baku street circuit, reignited the debate over how the FIA should police reckless behaviour in the sport’s most unforgiving environments.

The crash began when Colapinto, who was running in the midfield for the Red Bull‑affiliated team, mis‑judged his braking point into Turn 1 on the restart. His car spun across the racing line, forcing a chain reaction that saw several drivers, including Norris, Gasly and the Haas pair, collide or be forced off‑track. Both McLaren cars suffered severe damage, and Gasly’s Alpine was left with a puncture that forced an immediate retirement. In total, five cars were directly affected, and the incident prompted a virtual safety car before the race resumed under full green‑flag conditions.

Norris’s frustration was evident in the post‑race press conference, where he said, “I think he deserves at least a one‑race ban. It was a careless mistake that cost a lot of people a chance to finish the race.” His comments reflect a growing sentiment among drivers that the current penalty system does not adequately deter dangerous restarts, especially on circuits like Baku where the margins for error are razor‑thin. The track’s long straight and tight, high‑speed corners amplify any mis‑calculation, turning a simple spin into a potentially race‑ending incident.

The FIA’s disciplinary framework allows stewards to impose grid penalties, time penalties, or fines, but a suspension is rarely used in Formula 1. Historically, only the most egregious infractions—such as deliberate collisions or repeated dangerous conduct—have resulted in race bans. Colapinto, who is in his debut season and has shown flashes of speed in the lower formulas, has not been previously flagged for reckless driving. Nonetheless, the severity of the Baku crash, which eliminated two championship‑contending drivers, may push the governing body to reconsider the adequacy of its sanctions.

Team principals also weighed in. McLaren’s Zak Brown expressed disappointment, noting that “the loss of both cars on a restart is something we never want to see, and it’s especially painful when it’s caused by a driver still learning the ropes.” Alpine’s Laurent Team Bianchi, while sympathetic to Colapinto’s inexperience, emphasized the need for “clearer guidelines on restart protocols” to protect drivers and preserve the integrity of the competition. Both statements underline the fine line teams must walk between supporting their drivers’ development and demanding accountability for on‑track safety.

As the paddock heads into the next round in Monaco, the incident will likely be a focal point in the FIA’s post‑race review. If the stewards decide to issue a suspension, it would set a precedent that could reshape driver behaviour on restarts, particularly on street circuits where the stakes are high and the margins thin. Conversely, a lighter penalty might fuel calls for a more robust safety framework, perhaps incorporating mandatory training modules for new drivers on high‑risk tracks.

Looking ahead, the Baku crash serves as a stark reminder that even a single error can ripple through the field, affecting championship battles and driver careers alike. Whether the FIA opts for a stern sanction or a policy overhaul, the outcome will reverberate throughout the remainder of the season, influencing how teams and drivers approach the sport’s most perilous moments.
